absent: Numeric values and bit positions of operation presence flags and related dentry, inode and lookup flag bits.
Full memory layouts of dentry, inode, superblock, mount, file, qstr and external-name structures.
Behavior of allocation and lookup helpers not routed here such as anonymous, parallel and regular allocators and alias finders.
Hash table sizing, distribution policy, geometry computation and constant-folding mechanics.
Effects of security, notification and encryption hooks beyond the call sites shown.
Complete rename exclusion protocol and interaction with concurrent rename, lookup and directory mutation.
Eviction, pruning, reference counting and teardown lifecycle beyond the attach and move paths shown.
Boot ordering guarantees and failure handling for subsystem initializers whose bodies were not routed.
ABI stability promises for exported helpers beyond the observed stale, memory, loop, invalid and too-long cases.

findings.text: Alias acquisition services provide a disconnected entry for ordinary use and a root-tracked entry for roots through a shared helper, plus case-insensitive addition that first probes the hash and otherwise allocates either a parallel or regular entry before splicing.

Splice and attach services bind an inode to an entry. One variant uses default handling, another accepts caller supplied directory operations, a plain add path handles optional inode presence, and a new-inode path notifies security before binding and creation-state release.

Tree mutation and lookup services move one entry onto another under rename exclusion, exchange two entries, reinsert an entry into the hash, compute a filesystem-aware hash before lookup, release a parallel lookup with waiter wakeup, and report a parent inode number.

Transient file services assign a temporary label to an unlinked negative entry using either an inode-number derived form or a caller supplied label with length validation, then combine link-count adjustment with naming and binding.
Default operation installation records caller supplied directory operations on a superblock and refreshes the cached operation presence bits while preserving unrelated flag bits.

Operation presence bits derive solely from non-null handler pointers in the operations table. A grouped mask covers the full set of cache-relevant handlers. Per-entry and per-superblock state stores the derived bits, and installing operations on an entry that already carries them triggers a one-time warning.

Binding a freshly created inode requires a negative entry and a valid inode. The flow notifies security, attaches under combined guards, enforces that creation state is still set, orders visibility, then clears creation markers and wakes creation waiters.

Alias acquisition passes through error pointers, rejects a missing inode as stale, reuses any existing alias found before or under guard, otherwise allocates an anonymous entry, attaches it to the inode alias chain, optionally adds root membership when not disconnected, and consumes the caller reference on success while releasing it on all other paths.

Case-insensitive addition short-circuits when a hashed match already exists and releases the new inode. A parallel-lookup parent uses a parallel allocator and requires the result to remain in lookup, otherwise a regular allocator is used. Allocation failure yields a memory error, and a successful splice wakes and releases the intermediate entry.

Name lookup always starts from the generic full hash. A filesystem hash handler runs only when the directory advertises it, may leave the hash unchanged, and a negative handler result becomes an error pointer instead of proceeding to table lookup.

Splice reuses an existing directory alias only for directories. An ancestor relationship produces a rate-limited warning and a loop error. A non-root alias is relocated through the unalias helper, a root alias drops secondary root linkage if present before relocation, and all other cases fall through to hashed insertion.

Hashed insertion removes a parallel-lookup entry from its lookup table under a directory sequence window, optionally installs operations, links the alias and refreshes notification state under sequence-protected inode attachment when an inode is present, always rehashes, then closes the sequence and wakes lookup waiters.

Name storage distinguishes inline short buffers from shared external buffers with reference counts. Swapping exchanges external pointers, steals storage when only one side is external, exchanges inline words when both are internal, and always exchanges the combined hash and length field. Copying takes a reference on external sources and frees the prior external buffer when its last reference drops.

Encrypted-name move handling has two build configurations. One clears the no-key marker and conditionally clears the revalidation flag only when the active revalidator is the encryption revalidator. The other configuration performs no action.

Unaliasing within a shared parent needs no extra rename synchronization. Across parents it requires both the filesystem rename mutex and shared access to the alias parent, failing as stale when either is unavailable, plus optional filesystem unalias hooks that can veto the move. The relocation itself is non-exchanging.

Transient naming requires inline storage with a negative unlinked entry. The numeric form derives a label from the inode number, the caller-supplied form enforces a maximum inline length and appends termination, invalid preconditions yield an invalid-argument error and oversize names yield a name-too-long error.

Parent number reporting first attempts a read-side critical section with sequence validation around parent and inode reads. When the fast path cannot complete safely it falls back to holding the entry guard while reading through the stable parent link.

Attachment paths nest the inode guard outside the entry guard, with an additional superblock roots guard only while linking root membership. Whole-tree relocation holds rename exclusion across the operation, acquires parent guards in ancestor-aware order with nesting annotations, then locks both entries at fixed nesting levels and protects linkage changes with sequence counters.

Parallel lookup removal holds the entry guard while taking the bucket guard to clear lookup state and detach the lookup node. Waiter notification occurs while still holding the entry guard and clears the waiter flag after waking. Directory sequence windows disable preemption, spin until an even value can be advanced, and publish completion with release ordering before re-enabling preemption.

Entries progress among negative unhashed, parallel lookup, hashed, disconnected, secondary root, and unlinked transient states. Allocation creates unhashed or lookup entries, insertion and rehash publish them, relocation rewrites parent and sibling linkage, alias acquisition creates disconnected or root members, and transient naming precedes final binding.

Directory mutation sequencing uses even values for stable and odd values for in-progress. Starting a mutation waits for an even value and advances it by one, ending publishes the start value plus two. Observers retry when they witness an odd value or a changed sequence across the critical section.

Early cache setup initializes parallel-lookup buckets and conditionally allocates dentry and inode hash tables unless distribution defers allocation. Late setup creates slab caches for dentries, inodes, names, files and mounts, then performs deferred hash allocation and records table geometry for constant folding.

Mount initialization creates mount caches and hash tables, prepares device numbers, initializes kernel filesystem node caches and global locks, brings up system and shared-memory filesystems, builds the initial mount tree, and mounts a failure filesystem whose root path is retained, aborting boot when that mount fails.

File subsystem initialization creates regular and backing file object caches with type-safe reclaim and a global file counter, derives the maximum open-file count from available memory minus a reserve with a lower bound, and creates the pathname component cache with an embedded inline area.

Several misuse conditions abort execution: binding over a positive entry or without an inode, splicing onto a hashed entry, relocating an entry onto itself or onto its own descendant, and transient naming on an unsuitable entry. Exchange additionally warns on missing inodes or root participants.

Recoverable failures use error pointers or negative codes: stale inode on missing or contended alias work, memory exhaustion on anonymous or regular allocation, loop detection on ancestor splice, invalid argument on unsuitable transient targets, oversize names, and propagated filesystem hash errors.

A directory entry links to its inode through a per-inode alias chain, to its parent through sibling linkage, and optionally to superblock root membership. It carries operation pointers with presence flags, a sequence counter, a parallel-lookup node with waiter state, and either an inline short name or a reference-counted external name with combined hash and length.
Link-count reduction for transient files combines a link drop with a dirty marking. The transient-file flow applies that adjustment before assigning the transient label and binding the inode.
Dentry hash sizing accepts a boot-time unsigned numeric option with success reporting. Block-device cache setup is an empty operation in the routed configuration.
